Eggs of the Rainwater killifish (Lucania parva) incubated at a stable 25 °C [T = 25 °C] undergo a rapid period of embryonic development, culminating in eclosion after approximately 7.17 days [ab = approximately 7.17 days]. Upon hatching, the prolarvae measure just 0.49 cm [Lb = 0.49 cm] in total length, a diminutive size typical of fundulid species. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva relies on endogenous reserves, and its wet weight at this stage is a mere 0.000817 grams [Wwb = 0.000817 grams]. This initial mass is derived from the relatively small egg diameter of roughly 1.16 mm. The brief incubation period, compared to other cyprinodontiform fishes, likely reflects the selective pressures of the ephemeral, shallow-water habitats this species occupies, where rapid hatching may confer a survival advantage against fluctuating water levels and variable temperatures.

As the young-of-year transition from lecithotrophic larvae to actively feeding, exogenously feeding juveniles, their growth trajectory is remarkably steep. By the time individuals attain puberty, a critical developmental milestone marked by the onset of gametogenesis, they have reached a total length of 2.5 cm [Lp = 2.5 cm] and a corresponding wet weight of 0.22 grams [Wwp = 0.22 grams]. This weight represents a substantial increase from the birth mass, reflecting the efficient conversion of dietary zooplankton into somatic tissue. The onset of sexual maturation at this relatively modest size suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive investment, a pattern common among small-bodied, iteroparous fishes inhabiting unpredictable coastal environments, where adult mortality can be high.

Under laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 25 °C [T = 25 °C], a sexually mature female can achieve a remarkable maximum reproductive rate. Observations indicate she is capable of producing, on average, 104 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 104 eggs per clutch], and with an annual spawning frequency of approximately one spawning event per year [F_R_i = approximately one spawning event per year]. This high fecundity per event enables a single female to generate a substantial number of offspring over her lifetime, though the low annual frequency constrains the annual reproductive output. The ability to produce a clutch of this size is energetically demanding, relying on a continuous input of nutrients from the surrounding marsh environment, and it underscores the species’ role as a trophic link between primary production and higher-level consumers in its saltmarsh ecosystem.

The ultimate size achieved by the Rainwater killifish is modest, with the largest adults reaching a total length of 6.2 cm [Li = 6.2 cm]. This maximum, or asymptotic, length corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of 3.77 grams [Wwi = 3.77 grams], a size that is typically attained after the first year of life. This asymptotic size places Lucania parva among the smaller members of the Fundulidae family, a trait that correlates strongly with its short generation time and high population turnover rates. Field surveys in tidal creeks along the Gulf Coast consistently show that few individuals exceed this length, indicating that this size represents a physiological limit for the species rather than a sampling artifact, likely constrained by the resource availability of its niche.

Longevity data for the Rainwater killifish, derived from both mark-recapture studies and otolith analysis, indicate that individuals seldom survive beyond five years. Under the thermal conditions typical of its southern range, which average 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum recorded time since birth at death is approximately 1825 days [am = approximately 1825 days]. This five-year lifespan, while short in absolute terms, is relatively long when compared to other small cyprinodontids, many of which have a maximum longevity of only one to two years. The ability to live for half a decade allows for repeated, iteroparous spawning events across multiple seasons, thereby buffering the population against years of poor reproductive success. This demographic strategy, combining high fecundity with a moderate lifespan, appears well-suited to the stochastic salinity and temperature regimes of its coastal marsh habitat.
